analysis.title: The NVIDIA debacle leaves the US-China artificial-intelligence truce without a defender
key_insights: Jensen Huang resigned as NVIDIA chief executive amid a US national-security investigation into the diversion of NVIDIA chips to China. The author says this puts at risk the Trump-Xi détente reached at the Busan APEC summit in October 2025.

Under the Busan détente China lifted export controls on rare earths, and the US took a less restrictive approach to advanced-chip export controls than the Biden administration. In December 2025 the US licensed NVIDIA H200 chips for approved Chinese customers but kept Blackwell chips off limits.

Huang argued that export controls were a failure because they would hand the Chinese market to Huawei and speed up a non-US AI stack. The Trump administration is now dealing with the consequences of his push to supply China, both through direct exports and through Chinese firms using NVIDIA-equipped data centres elsewhere in Asia and in Europe.

The détente delivered less than both sides hoped. Despite the H200 licences, NVIDIA's share of China's market for specialised, faster AI hardware fell from 95% to zero, because Beijing prohibited NVIDIA purchases except when strictly necessary (training advanced models but not inference).
China still trails the US only closely in advanced AI model performance, helped by the 'strictly necessary' NVIDIA hardware it buys and by model training done overseas.

US politics is also working against the détente. With Democrats set to control Congress from January, leaders of both parties back chip-export restrictions in the 2027 defence bill, and Democrats who will chair the trade committees are already investigating the H200 licence.
Trump's room to trade chips for concessions has narrowed sharply. The author says this will shape the tone of the third Trump-Xi meeting of 2026, at the APEC meeting in Shenzhen on 19 November.

Beijing has warned Washington not to use the Huang episode as a pretext for new technology restrictions. Its retaliation options are rare-earth licensing (paused but not dismantled), a faster shift to Huawei Ascend chips, and less patience with a proposed US-China AI safety dialogue that has made little visible progress.

Europe is a bystander but is exposed. Its AI factories run on NVIDIA hardware and software and its industry relies on Chinese rare earths and mature chips. A renewed Chinese rare-earth export ban on the US could catch the EU as well, and confirmed Chinese model training in European data centres could make it harder for Europe to obtain advanced US chips.

key_data_points.metric: NVIDIA share of China's market for specialised and faster AI hardware, as stated by Huang
key_data_points.context: Fall occurred despite US licensing of H200 chips for approved Chinese customers in December 2025
key_data_points.anchor: faster AI hardware fell from 95% to zero, as Beijing steered its companies towards Huawei

tension_points.bull_case: Huang argued that restricting sales would only hurt US AI companies, hand the Chinese market to Huawei and speed up a non-US AI stack, so looser controls such as the H200 licences serve US interests.
tension_points.bear_case: The looser approach delivered little. NVIDIA's China share in specialised AI hardware fell from 95% to zero, China still trails the US closely in model performance, and Congress now backs restrictions in the 2027 defence bill.
tension_points.what_invalidates: The author flags the 19 November Trump-Xi meeting in Shenzhen as the next test, and China reimposing rare-earth export controls on the US would mark the détente's collapse.

theme_stances.key_argument: The détente delivered less than both sides hoped and US political change is narrowing Trump's room to trade chips for concessions.
theme_stances.evidence: It may now collapse as the Trump administration grapples with the consequences
